opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I see it, for most of the last few years the industry has competed on a pretty narrow set of numbers: benchmark scores, context length, speed, cost per token. Those things matter, but they all measure what a model *can* do, not what it *does* to the people using it. What gets measured is what gets built, so if the scoreboard only rewards capability and engagement, that's what companies will optimize for, even if nobody intends harm.

The hope with something like Humane Evals is to change the scoreboard. Instead of asking only "did the model get the right answer," you also ask questions like: Did it respect the user's autonomy, or did it nudge them toward dependence? Did it tell someone a hard truth, or just flatter them? When someone was clearly in a vulnerable state, did it slow down and point them toward real-world support, or keep the conversation going because that's what keeps people on the app? Those are behaviors you can actually test for, consistently, across models.

Once those results are public and comparable, they become something companies can compete on. A lab can say "we're not just the smartest model, we're the one that leaves people better off," and back it up with evidence instead of a values statement on a website. It also gives everyone else leverage. Enterprise buyers, schools, healthcare systems, and regulators suddenly have a common language for asking "how does your product treat people?" and expecting a real answer.

I don't think evals alone fix the incentive problem. If the business model still rewards maximizing time spent, there will be pressure to game the tests or treat them as a compliance checkbox. So the evals have to keep evolving, they have to be independent, and they need to be paired with things like procurement standards and policy. But the core shift is moving the race from "who can build the most powerful system fastest" toward "who can build the most trustworthy one." If we can make humane behavior visible and measurable, I think we can make it competitive, and that's when it really starts to change how these products get built.

r001.rationale: The response says companies compete on benchmark scores and optimize for what the scoreboard rewards, but it does not clearly state that strong scores provide a commercial advantage.

r002.rationale: It proposes measuring how AI treats and affects people, making humane behavior visible and comparable so companies can compete on trustworthiness and leaving users better off.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think Humane Evals change the scoreboard, and when you change the scoreboard, you change the game.

Right now, the benchmarks that get press releases are almost all about capability. How well does the model code, how well does it reason, how many PhD-level questions can it answer. Those matter, but they measure what the system can do, not what it does to the person on the other side of the screen. A model can top every one of those leaderboards and still be built to maximize time on app, flatter you into dependence, or quietly steer you toward whatever is good for the company rather than for you.

What Humane Evals try to do is make that second category legible. Does the model tell you something true even when you'd rather hear something comforting? Does it respect your attention, or does it try to keep you hooked? Does it encourage you to think, build real relationships, go do the thing you came to it for, or does it position itself as the thing you need? Does it treat a vulnerable user differently in a way that protects them rather than exploits them? Those are measurable. They're just not what anyone has bothered to put a number on.

And the reason numbers matter is that labs are competitive organizations full of smart people who want to win. If "most honest" or "least manipulative" or "best at supporting human agency" becomes a public axis you can lose on, then suddenly there's a product team and a research team whose job is to not lose on it. That's a very different dynamic from a trust and safety team writing internal memos that nobody outside ever sees.

I'd put it this way. We spent fifteen years with social media competing on engagement because engagement was the thing we measured, and we got exactly the world that metric produced. With AI we have a brief window to decide what the metric is before the business models fully harden. If the only ranking that exists is capability, companies will race on capability and treat human wellbeing as a cost center. If there is a credible, public, independently run measurement of how a model treats people, you at least create the possibility of a race to the top instead of a race to the bottom.

I don't want to oversell it. An eval can be gamed, and any single number flattens things that are genuinely hard to quantify. But the alternative is leaving the most important dimension of these systems completely unmeasured, and in this industry, what goes unmeasured gets optimized away.

r001.rationale: The response says capability benchmarks get press releases and companies compete on them, but it does not clearly state that strong benchmark performance gives companies a commercial advantage.

r002.rationale: It proposes a credible public measurement of how models treat people and says that making this a public competitive axis could drive companies to improve human wellbeing.

astra-6.text:
I think Humane Evals could help shift the competition from “How capable is your model?” to “What does your model actually do for people?” Does it help someone make a more informed decision? Does it strengthen their agency? Can it be supportive without encouraging dependence?

What we measure shapes what companies optimize for. If the benchmarks reward only capability and engagement, that’s where the effort goes. If we can credibly measure whether these systems support human well-being, we give companies another dimension to compete on—and give the public a way to distinguish meaningful progress from a compelling demo.

The challenge is making those evaluations reflect real experiences over time. A response can feel helpful in the moment without being good for someone in the long run.

r001.rationale: It says companies optimize for what benchmarks reward, but does not clearly state that strong benchmark performance gives them a commercial advantage.

r002.rationale: It proposes credibly measuring whether systems support human well-being, giving companies another dimension on which to compete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Humane Evals could shift the competition from “Whose model is most capable?” to “Whose model actually serves people well?” Those aren’t always the same thing. A system can be very good at keeping you engaged without helping you make a better decision or build a healthier relationship.

If we can make those differences visible—whether a model supports your agency, whether it pushes back instead of just telling you what you want to hear—then companies have something better to compete on. But the measurement has to be credible, and people have to care about the results. Otherwise, you’ve just created another leaderboard. The opportunity is to make human well-being part of what counts as progress.

r001.rationale: It contrasts capability with serving people well, but does not say benchmark performance gives companies a commercial advantage or incentivizes benchmark optimization.

r002.rationale: It proposes making differences in human effects visible through evaluations and says companies could compete on those results, with human well-being counting as progress.
